question.prompt: On an examination of \(n\) questions a student answers correctly \(15\) of the first \(20.\) Of the remaining questions he answers one third correctly. All the questions have the same credit. If the student’s mark is \(50\%,\) how many different values of \(n\) can there be?

solutions.explanation:
Because every question has the same credit, a mark of \(50\%\) means that exactly half the questions were answered correctly. Let \(n\) be the total number of questions, an integer with \(n\ge20\).

There are \(n-20\) questions after the first twenty, and one third of these were answered correctly. Thus the total number of correct answers gives the equation
\[
15+\frac{n-20}{3}=\frac n2.
\]
Multiplying every term by \(6\) clears the denominators:
\[
90+2(n-20)=3n.
\]
Therefore \(50+2n=3n\), so \(n=50\).

This value satisfies the counting conditions: the remaining \(30\) questions contribute \(10\) correct answers, giving \(15+10=25\) correct out of \(50\). Every possible total must satisfy the equation, and its only solution works. Hence there is exactly \(1\) possible value of \(n\), choice D.
solutions.title: Count the correct answers in two ways
